introduction: Scholar, campaigner, writer and constitutional thinker: B. R. Ambedkar approached equality through education, public action and the institutions of democracy. These moments offer a way into that larger story. Each account leads back to a source, including the books you can read here.

events.title: A life shaped by the struggle for dignity
events.summary: Born in 1891, Ambedkar would confront exclusion in everyday life and pursue education across continents.
paragraphs: An editorial note in Volume 10 gives Ambedkar’s birth date as 14 April 1891, referring to his school register at Satara. The accompanying account describes discrimination reaching into ordinary childhood experiences: obtaining water, washing clothes and travelling to meet family.

The same account follows his education at Elphinstone College and the scholarship support of the ruler of Baroda. It records an offer to study overseas after graduation. Read these episodes together to see how the archive connects barriers to basic dignity with opportunities for further study.

events.title: A wider world of ideas
events.summary: Study at Columbia brought Ambedkar into conversation with economics, politics and democratic thought.
paragraphs: Ambedkar arrived at Columbia University in July 1913. Columbia’s South Asia Institute records his master’s degree in 1915 and his PhD in 1927. These dates distinguish his period of study from the later formal award of the doctorate.

Among his teachers was John Dewey. Columbia’s account places this education within Ambedkar’s continuing importance as a democratic thinker and constitutional lawyer. In 1952 the university also awarded him an honorary LL.D. His university years are one entry point into the global range of his intellectual life.

sources.label: Columbia University, South Asia Institute · ICLS Ambedkar Initiative

events.title: Water, citizenship and the Mahad struggle
events.summary: A public water tank became the focus of a struggle to make equal civic rights a reality.
paragraphs: The Mahad account in Volume 17 describes a peaceful march to the Chawdar Tank. Ambedkar drank water there, and others followed. The action asserted a right that caste exclusion had denied despite a municipal resolution opening the tank.

The chapter also records opposition and violence after the march. Later documents describe preparations for renewed action in December 1927. This was more than an isolated dispute about access to water: the account itself frames the struggle in terms of civic rights, human dignity and exclusion from public life.

events.title: The Poona Pact and political representation
events.summary: The agreement became a lasting point of debate about how oppressed communities could secure a political voice.
paragraphs: Volume 5 records the signing of the Poona Pact on 24 September 1932. It reproduces a resolution from a public meeting the following day supporting the agreement and calling for withdrawal of the separate-electorate decision within the Hindu community.

The surrounding discussion is critical of the settlement and records opposition to it among the communities it concerned. This source should therefore be read as an argument about the consequences of the pact, alongside the reproduced resolution. It opens a central question in Ambedkar’s work: what arrangements make political representation effective?

events.title: A speech that became Annihilation of Caste
events.summary: An undelivered address became one of Ambedkar’s most influential published works.
paragraphs: Ambedkar prepared Annihilation of Caste for a 1936 meeting of Hindu caste reformers. Columbia’s account explains that the organizers withdrew their invitation after seeing the draft. Ambedkar then published the work himself.

The local Volume 1 contains the work together with a reply to Mahatma Gandhi. Its title page identifies the reproduced text as the third edition of 1944. That distinction matters: the work originated in 1936, while this collected edition presents a later version. Follow the local source to read the argument in full.

events.title: What makes a constitution work?
events.summary: In the Assembly, Ambedkar connected constitutional forms with the habits needed to sustain democracy.
paragraphs: In the 4 November 1948 debate, Ambedkar discussed constitutional morality while presenting the Draft Constitution. His explanation connected respect for constitutional forms with open criticism of public authorities and confidence that political opponents would respect those same forms.

He also linked the form of administration to the form of the Constitution. The passage invites a question that reaches beyond the written document: what practices make constitutional government work? The local debate and collected writings let you follow the argument in its original setting.

sources.label: Constituent Assembly debate · 4 November 1948 · PDF page 42

events.title: Liberty, equality and fraternity together
events.summary: Ambedkar urged India to give political democracy a social foundation.
paragraphs: Near the conclusion of the Assembly’s work, Ambedkar argued that political democracy needed social democracy beneath it. He described liberty, equality and fraternity as connected principles of life, rather than separate ideals that could safely be taken apart.

The passage explains the dangers of liberty without equality and equality without liberty. Fraternity gives the other principles a basis in relations between people. Reading this argument connects constitutional design with the social conditions in which citizens actually live.

events.title: Embracing Buddhism at Nagpur
events.summary: Ambedkar’s turn to Buddhism became a major public event, documented through statements and programmes.
paragraphs: A statement dated 23 September 1956 announced that Ambedkar’s conversion to Buddhism would take place at Nagpur on 14 October. Volume 17 preserves the announcement and documents the preparations around it.

The reproduced programme lists the conversion ceremony, the participation of Chandramani Mahasthavir, and a public address by Ambedkar the following morning. These records show how the event was organized and communicated. Read them alongside the account of the conversion and Ambedkar’s writings on Buddhism to explore its wider meaning.
